extracted.intended_audience: creative writers seeking peer feedback, beta readers, critique partners, or evaluating online critique platforms
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for authors on the multi-stage manuscript development process (alpha → beta → critique), how to recruit and use beta readers and critique partners, and what to evaluate when choosing an online critique platform (example: Scribophile).

rubrics_metrics.name: Writing process stages (alpha, beta, critique)
rubrics_metrics.description: The author outlines a three-stage development process: alpha (research, drafting, self-editing), beta (target-audience subjective feedback), then critique (objective critique/critique partners).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do stages in order: complete self-edits first, then test audience reaction in beta, then fix objective issues with critique partners. The post uses these stage labels and explains why the ordering matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alpha stage: research, draft, self-edit (at least three self-edits)
rubrics_metrics.description: Before getting outside feedback, a manuscript should be researched, drafted, and self-edited in at least three stages to reach a readable baseline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do enough on your own so you aren’t embarrassed to have people read it; the alpha stage is where you make it 'readable' before beta testing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beta stage: target-audience subjective feedback
rubrics_metrics.description: Beta readers must be members of the manuscript's target audience and give real, honest, subjective opinions about whether they'd read/buy the work and why.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask open subjective questions like 'What do you like/dislike? Would you buy it and why or why not?' Beta feedback is about building a target audience, not objective technical fixes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beta-stage sampling recommendation: two rounds of ten readers each
rubrics_metrics.description: For a good beta stage the author recommends at least two rounds of ten readers each, with an edit between rounds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This provides a larger sample to reach a consensus; expect 20 different subjective responses and use the pattern of responses, not one-offs, to guide changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid hubris: internalize essential feedback
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors must avoid dismissing critical beta feedback out of pride; you asked for help because you need it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize when negative feedback indicates real problems with the manuscript and accept that you aren't the final arbiter simply because you wrote it ('Bitch, you ain’t -insert rich author-').

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't follow every suggestion; seek consensus and make editorial calls
rubrics_metrics.description: Beta feedback will be contradictory; you should look for consensus rather than trying to satisfy every individual comment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If 19 readers like something and 1 hates it for a subjective reason, you can discard that one recommendation. Use majority patterns to decide what to change; 'make a call' when feedback conflicts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critique stage: objective issues and critique partners
rubrics_metrics.description: The critique stage (critique partners) focuses on objective, technical issues: plot holes, timeline errors, internal consistency (e.g., magic systems), factual/research errors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critique partners should answer 'Did I do this right?' rather than 'Would you read this?' They help ensure internal logic and accuracy so the work doesn't look foolish to knowledgeable readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value specialist critique partners for technical accuracy
rubrics_metrics.description: A critique partner who is an expert in a subject area (e.g., history, physics) is valuable for catching factual mistakes and rare issues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appreciate and prioritize critique partners who know the topic — their input prevents obvious errors that could be publicly embarrassing or undermine credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Order matters: do beta before deep technical critique
rubrics_metrics.description: Do beta (subjective audience validation) before investing in deep, time-consuming technical edits or research-heavy rewrites.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: if beta readers reject your setting or premise, you may need to change it completely — doing technical work first can waste time if the book's core concept doesn't resonate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critique partners should help you write the book you intended
rubrics_metrics.description: The goal of critique partners is to help realize the author's original intentions by finding objective mismatches between intention and execution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: They are not hired to make the book more marketable per se but to ensure the manuscript does what the author intended in a technically correct way.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specific objective checklist for critiques
rubrics_metrics.description: When critiquing, check for plot holes, timeline errors, magic-system internal consistency, and accuracy of research or technical details.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are non-subjective correctness items that can be fixed; the post gives examples (time travel/timeline mistakes, bad heat physics, inconsistent magic rules).

rubrics_metrics.name: Beta vs critique distinction: subjective vs objective
rubrics_metrics.description: Beta readers answer subjective market/audience questions (Do people connect? Would they buy?), critique partners answer objective craft questions (Did I do this right?).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use beta to confirm audience, then use critique partners to fix craft; do not conflate the two stages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Platform promise: guaranteed critiques (Scribophile's 'three critiques' guarantee)
rubrics_metrics.description: Scribophile advertises that posted work will receive at least three critiques before moving out of the queue; the site uses a points system where you earn points by critiquing others to post your own work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: On paper this seems good: incentivizes mutual critique. But the author warns the promise can be undermined by user behavior and design flaws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality requirement for critiques on a platform
rubrics_metrics.description: A good critique must be specific to the posted work and not a generic or copy/pasted text designed only to game the points system.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-patterns include copy/paste critiques, bot-like replies, or critiques from people who didn't read author notes/target audience; platforms must discourage 'fishing for points'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Platform moderation and safety expectation
rubrics_metrics.description: An online critique platform should have adequate moderation and remove illegal or abusive content (e.g., hate speech, child pornography); lack of oversight is unacceptable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author reports extreme illegal content remained visible and a site response that 'we do not moderate' — the post treats that as a major failure and safety risk.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effective reporting and content-removal process
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporting mechanisms should be timely and effective; slow, human-error prone processes that leave illegal content live are insufficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author experienced slow responses and content remaining visible after reports; platforms should have faster moderation workflows and/or automated safeguards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ability for authors to curate comments/feedback
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors should be able to remove or curate critiques on their work (e.g., hide unhelpful or abusive comments) without penalizing legitimate critiquers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern on Scribophile: deleting a comment also deletes the points earned by the critiquer, which prevents authors from curating. Paid users expect tools to manage their feedback.

rubrics_metrics.name: Group moderation limitations on volunteer-run groups
rubrics_metrics.description: Groups led by volunteer users (not platform staff) cannot fully police all content; group moderators can delete threads but may not control comments on posted work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Relying solely on volunteer moderators leaves gaps; platform-level moderation is needed for safety and consistent enforcement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Platform UX and visibility design should reward, not punish, good critiquers
rubrics_metrics.description: Site layout and algorithms should not reduce exposure for users who provide quality critiques; design choices that move good critiquers 'under the fold' are counterproductive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author observed being penalized (moved lower) for 'good critiquer' status, cutting engagement — platforms should design for fair exposure and retention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paid membership should deliver moderation, development, and useful features
rubrics_metrics.description: If a site charges for memberships, the fees should fund moderation, web development, and functional features; lack of visible investment raises concerns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author questions why Scribophile charges if it lacks moderation and has poor UX; suggests free alternatives (Critique Circle, Twitter) that may offer oversight without cost.

rubrics_metrics.name: Users gaming points systems undermines guaranteed-critique promises
rubrics_metrics.description: Points-for-critique economies can be gamed by users posting minimal or copy/paste 'critiques' to earn points and post their own work, undermining quality guarantees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Platforms need checks against gaming (reporting, moderation, quality verification) because otherwise guarantees (e.g., 'three critiques') are hollow.

rubrics_metrics.name: When platform fails on safety/ethics, escalate (police, payment stop)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a platform tolerates illegal or egregiously harmful content and fails to act, escalate by filing law enforcement reports and seeking refunds or stopping payment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author called police and initiated a bank stop-payment after reporting the content and being refused a refund; this is presented as an option when platform-level remedies fail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer platforms with oversight and community reporting that actually removes abusive content
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose critique platforms or communities that enforce standards and can remove abusive content quickly; public social platforms with moderation (Twitter, WordPress) may offer better recourse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author recommends using Twitter/#writingcommunity or Critique Circle as alternatives with better oversight rather than paying for a poorly-moderated site.
